new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (24 pp, printed pp.123-146) and the page render. The quoted sentence is on printed p.141, Appendix, second paragraph after the source-village list, verbatim: "With regard to the phonetic notation, stress is penultimate unless other-wise marked." (extracted text of the chapter file page 19 and of page 147 both give it; the page scan shows it with capital W). Locator correction only: it is PDF page 19 of the chapter file, not "PDF page 13" (page 13 is printed p.135, the concluding remarks); the full-volume page 147 given by the compiler is right. Surrounding section read: the Appendix presents a Blust-revised 200-item list for six languages (Seti, Bobot, Masiwang, Geser, Watubela, Band…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the penultimate syllable; a small number of words (marked with an acute in the wordlist) have final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-penultimate stress is 'otherwise marked' in the lists: in the Watubela column a few words carry an acute on the final syllable (read from the page scan: mamán 'say', katlú 'egg', malá: 'long', kotnáu 'where', laŋit ni tái 'cloud', sabóu 'sit'), so final stress occurs in a minority of lexical items.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a 200-item comparative wordlist; the statement is a transcription convention covering all six languages of the appendix (Seti, Bobot, Masiwang, Geser, Watubela, Banda), with the Watubela data from Efa village (Watubela Island) and occasional Keldor (K) forms; it is Collins's own field data (two years of fieldwork), not a phonological analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Collins 1986's Watubela data are from Efa village on Watubela Island proper (with some forms from Keldor, marked K); Ethnologue/Glottolog treat Kesui (Kasiui) and Watubela as dialects of the single language watu1247, so no separate glottocode applies. The 19th-century 'Matabello' wordlists (Wallace 1869) are, per Collins 1986 fn.7, from Kesui island, and von Rosenberg 1867 p.106 already reports a dialect difference between Kassoewie (Kesui) and Watoebella. The stress statement is a notation convention that Collins applies jointly to all six Eastern Seram languages in his appendix, not a Watubela-specific phonological analysis.

sources.note: Comparative/subgrouping paper with a 200-item wordlist of six Eastern Seram languages incl. Watubela (Efa village; K = Keldor). Appendix p.141: 'With regard to the phonetic notation, stress is penultimate unless otherwise marked.' In the Watubela column (pp.142-145) a handful of words carry an acute on the final syllable (as read from the page scan: mamán 'say', katlú 'egg', malá: 'long', kotnáu 'where', laŋit ni tái 'cloud', sabóu 'sit'), i.e. marked exceptions with final stress. Body of the paper discusses only segmental sound changes (e.g. *a > o in the penultimate syllable).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page watu1247 (Watubela); Wikipedia 'Watubela language'
sources.note: Glottolog cites only Collins 1986 for subclassification (plus Ethnologue 2025 for status); names Esiriun, Kasiui, Kasui, Kesui, Matabello, Snabi Watubela, Wesi. Wikipedia cites Collins 1986, Loski & Loski 1989 and Grimes & Edwards (2026, survey of the Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste); neither says anything about stress. Crossref/Garuda queries for 'Watubela' returned only non-linguistic Indonesian local-government papers;org and the Internet Archive).
